title: Industrial systems and where factories locate

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: What an industrial system is - inputs, processes and outputs (products and waste) - and the factors that decide where factories and industrial zones are located. A worked case study of a real factory follows in the next section.

blocks.heading: An industrial system has three parts
blocks.text: Every factory, cannery or workshop is an industrial system with three parts. Inputs are what goes in: raw materials, labour, energy and capital - the money and machines the system needs. Processes are what happens inside: the making, heating, assembling and packing that change raw materials into products. Outputs are what comes out: the products the system sells, and the waste it creates while making them - gases from chimneys, waste water released or dumped, and solid waste such as offcuts and packaging. The parts connect in one direction: the processes consume the inputs and release the outputs.

blocks.heading: Processing changes the material
blocks.text: Processing means changing a raw material into a new product, and the change is what makes it processing: clay becomes bricks, pilchards become tinned fish, logs become planks. Any flow in a system diagram can be sorted with one test: does it go into the factory, or come out of it? Fish landed at the quay is an input; sealed tins on a pallet are an output. Defining the processes as "the processing" explains nothing - write what is done to the material, in what order, and what leaves at the other end. The flows balance, too: what enters the system leaves again, either as product or as waste.

blocks.heading: A worked system: a fish cannery
blocks.text: The pilchard canneries of Walvis Bay show the system in rounded figures. Inputs: about 40 000 tonnes of fish a year, tins, oil and salt, labour from the town, and energy for the canning lines. Processes: the fish are cleaned, cooked, packed into tins, sealed and labelled. Outputs: around 32 000 tonnes of canned fish and roughly 8 000 tonnes of waste - heads, skins and trimmings sold on as fishmeal, plus waste water and steam. Four fifths of the intake by mass leaves as product, one fifth as waste. Reading the three rows together is the point: the table is a system, and the numbers on either side of the processes must add up.

blocks.heading: The factors that decide where a factory goes
blocks.text: Factories locate where the balance of factors favours them: raw materials, labour, energy supply, transport routes, markets, flat land and government policy. Each factor should be given its direction in an answer. A bulk-losing industry such as copper smelting or cement sits beside its raw material, because most of the material's mass is discarded in processing and hauling ore is costly. A bakery sits in its market town, because loaves are bulkier and perishable compared with the flour they come from. A footloose industry using light, valuable components may prefer a motorway junction or a city with skilled workers. Government policy can tip the balance: tax breaks and serviced industrial estates have drawn factories to particular towns that raw materials alone would not have.

blocks.heading: Location is not impact
blocks.text: Two errors appear again and again in answers on this topic. The first is answering a location question with the factory's impacts - jobs created, noise made, dust raised - which describes what the factory does here rather than why it is here. The second is choosing an example at the wrong scale: a whole country cannot serve as an industrial zone, because a case study needs a named factory or estate with place-specific detail - small enough to be marked on a town map.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: Industry carries the development story of topic 3.1, where employment structure shifts from primary to secondary to tertiary jobs. Factories draw on energy from topic 3.5 and water from topic 3.6, sit in the urban settlements of topic 1.6, and their wastes feed the environmental risks of topic 3.7. Food processing links back to the farming systems of topic 3.2.
